title: Analysis of the 2028/2029 RPM Base Residual Auction - Part A
author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
claim: Data-center load (existing plus forecast) is the primary reason for PJM's tight supply, capacity shortfalls and high capacity prices; there would have been no shortfall in the last three auctions but for forecast data-center load.
method: Counterfactual re-clearing of the actual auction supply curve with the data-center portion of PJM's peak-load forecast removed (Scenario 4: existing+forecast data-center load removed; Scenario 3: only forecast growth removed). Estimates are lower than they would be without the auction's price floor.
notes: Table 1 of this report is the single best source for the per-auction data-center cost series. A circulating '2027/28 ~ $6.3bn' figure does not match the IMM: 2027/28 is $6.50bn (all data-center load) or $6.24bn (forecast growth only); $6.27bn is the 2028/29 figure. Auction revenue is not identical to cost to load (self-supply and bilateral hedges).

title: Analysis of the 2025/2026 RPM Base Residual Auction - Part G (Revised)
author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
claim: Inclusion of existing and forecast data-center load in the peak-load forecast raised 2025/26 capacity auction revenues by about $9.3bn.
method: Counterfactual re-clearing (Scenarios 87/88) removing data-center load from the 2024 PJM load forecast.
notes: Numbers verified from Table 1 of the IMM 2028/29 Part A, which cites this report; PDF also saved in data/raw/markets.

title: Analysis of the 2027/2028 RPM Base Residual Auction - Part A
author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
claim: Data-center load raised 2027/28 auction revenues by about $6.5bn; cumulative impact of the last three auctions above $23bn.
method: Counterfactual re-clearing with data-center load removed from PJM's 2025 load forecast.
notes: Also cited by Maryland OPC's FERC complaint ('more than $6.5 billion' and 'over $23 billion over the last three auctions').

title: 2025 State of the Market Report for PJM, Section 5: Capacity Market
author_org: Monitoring Analytics (Independent Market Monitor for PJM)
claim: RPM capacity revenue jumped from $2.6bn (2024/25 delivery year) to $14.9bn (2025/26) and $16.1-16.4bn for 2026/27-2027/28; annual capacity charges to load rose from $2.5bn to $14.8bn.
method: Market data (cleared MW x clearing prices; zonal net load prices after CTR credits).
notes: Descriptive (sizes the capacity bill), not an attribution study by itself.

title: Data Center Growth Could Increase Electricity Bills 8% Nationally and as Much as 25% in Some Regional Markets
author_org: Carnegie Mellon University & NC State University (Open Energy Outlook Initiative): Blackhurst, Wade, DeCarolis, de Queiroz, Johnson, Jaramillo
claim: Data-center and crypto-mining growth through 2030 could raise average US electricity generation costs 8%, with central and northern Virginia above 25%; keeps >25 GW of coal running and raises power-sector CO2 30%.
method: TEMOA-based Open Energy Outlook capacity-expansion model with and without projected data-center/crypto load, current policies.
notes: The 8% is a generation-cost increase that press often reports as 'bills'. A 2026 peer-reviewed version (Environmental Research Letters, NC State release May 2026) reportedly gives a 6-29% national range and up to 57% locally and 'up to 28%' CO2; that release returned HTTP 403 and is UNVERIFIED.

title: Connection Costs: Loophole Costs Customers Over $4 Billion to Connect Data Centers to Power Grid (policy brief + appendix)
author_org: Union of Concerned Scientists (Mike Jacobs)
claim: Utilities in seven PJM states approved $4.36bn of transmission projects in 2024 solely to connect individual data centers; over 95% of the projects pass all costs to all customers through formula transmission rates.
method: Review of utilities' PJM local/supplemental transmission plan submissions (TEAC/SRRTEP) and RTEP reports for projects whose need is a single large customer.
region: PJM: IL, MD, NJ, OH, PA, VA, WV
notes: Counts only direct connection (supplemental) projects, not regional backbone upgrades. These costs are spread by FERC formula rates, which do not track which customer caused them.

title: Extracting Profits from the Public: How Utility Ratepayers Are Paying for Big Tech's Power
author_org: Harvard Law School Electricity Law Initiative (Eliza Martin, Ari Peskoe)
claim: Utility rate structures, confidential special contracts and the federal/state transmission cost-allocation gap let utilities shift data-center costs to captive ratepayers while utilities profit from new rate base.

key_numbers.examples_cited: Oncor 82 GW potential DC load; AEP expects >=15 GW new DC load by 2030 on a 35 GW system peak; industry 2030 DC forecasts rose from 16 GW to 65 GW within 2024

method: Legal and regulatory analysis of ~50 state PUC proceedings on data-center rates and special contracts.
notes: Qualitative: it does not estimate a dollar amount of cost shift. Recommends special contracts that cover cost of service, tariffs for all new data centers, disclosure of forecasts, and flexible-operation requirements.

title: Factors Impacting Retail Electricity Prices in the United States (and 2025/2026 data updates)
author_org: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory & The Brattle Group (Wiser, Barbose, Cappers et al.; Hledik et al.)
claim: 2019-2024: states with the highest load growth generally saw real retail prices fall (fixed costs spread over more sales); distribution/transmission spending, storms/wildfires, RPS costs and gas prices drove increases. PJM is the exception: accelerated load growth plus supply and delivery constraints raised capacity prices.
method: State-level descriptive analysis plus regression of 2019-2024 price changes on candidate drivers (FERC Form 1, EIA-861).
notes: Authors warn past relationship may not persist where supply/delivery is constrained. Primary pages: https://emp.lbl.gov/retail-electricity-price-trends-and-drivers (LBL PDFs returned HTTP 403 to scripts; read the January 2026 deck from the Montana Legislature mirror). A July 2026 update with a load-growth deep dive exists but was not read (403).

title: Tailored for Scale: Amazon Data Center Case Studies (Ratepayer Study)
author_org: Energy and Environmental Economics (E3), funded by Amazon
claim: The Amazon data centers studied pay utility bills that meet or exceed their incremental cost to serve, producing surplus revenue that can put downward pressure on other customers' rates.
method: Facility-level revenue vs marginal cost-to-serve and directly assignable interconnection costs using Amazon-provided data.
notes: Funded and reviewed by Amazon. Does not model system-wide costs (regional transmission, capacity-market price effects) triggered by aggregate data-center growth, which is the IMM's main channel.

title: Understanding the Drivers of Rising Electricity Rates and the Role of Data Centers
author_org: Energy and Environmental Economics (E3), funded by the Data Center Coalition
claim: No quantitative evidence to date that data centers have been subsidized by other customers; states with the most load growth (TX, VA) had the smallest rate increases; in PJM, load growth (mainly data centers) explains about half of the 2024/25 to 2025/26 capacity price jump.
method: Literature review plus E3 decomposition of the PJM 2024/25 vs 2025/26 auction and review of large-load tariff database (Halcyon).
notes: Sponsor (DCC) reviewed the paper before publication. Note the tension with the IMM: E3 attributes ~50% of the 2025/26 increase to load growth and ~50% to market-design changes and retirements; the IMM's counterfactual attributes $9.3bn of $14.7bn (~63%) to data-center load.

title: Large Load Tariff Whitepaper (benchmarking representative large-load tariffs)
author_org: Energy and Environmental Economics (E3)
claim: Annual bills for an identical hypothetical data-center load differ materially across utility large-load tariffs; minimum-demand/contract-capacity provisions shift ramp-up risk onto the data center, protecting other customers.
method: Bill modeling of a standardized load shape under currently effective or recently approved large-load tariffs.
notes: Useful for the 'who pays' panel; detailed per-tariff numbers are in figures not extracted here.

title: Data Centers in Virginia (JLARC Report 598; E3 grid and rate modeling)
author_org: Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission, with E3
claim: Current rates allocate costs appropriately (no historic cost shift), but unconstrained data-center growth will raise generation and transmission costs that are hard to assign, putting upward pressure on residential bills.
method: E3 capacity-expansion and cost-of-service modeling for Dominion under several data-center growth scenarios (real dollars, G&T only, excludes distribution and inflation).
notes: Press summaries cite 'nearly $40/month' or '$444/yr by 2040'; those figures were not found in the presentation text read here (UNVERIFIED). Full report: https://jlarc.virginia.gov/pdfs/reports/Rpt598.pdf

title: Large load tariffs: a looming challenge for utilities (and follow-up on clean transition tariffs)
author_org: Wood Mackenzie (Ben Hertz-Shargel)
claim: Large-load tariffs (minimum contract terms, exit fees, collateral) are utilities' attempt to contain cost and risk but fall short for long-lived generation and transmission; transmission costs are hardest to confine to the large customer.
method: Review of utility large-load tariff provisions.
notes: Full report not accessed; claim from Wood Mackenzie opinion page snippet, Utility Dive and Resources Radio summaries. No quantitative result recorded.

title: AI Data Centers Are Sending Power Bills Soaring
author_org: Bloomberg News (graphics/analysis)
claim: Wholesale electricity prices at grid nodes near data-center clusters rose up to 267% over five years; many of the biggest jumps (e.g., Baltimore) are near data-center hot spots.
method: Node-level LMP comparison across seven RTOs against proximity to data-center activity.
notes: Paywalled; numbers from secondary coverage (Tom's Hardware, Sherwood, PolitiFact). Correlation, not causation; wholesale energy is roughly 30-50% of a retail bill and 2020 was a pandemic low-price baseline.

title: Fact-check: Elizabeth Warren on data centers and rising electricity costs
author_org: PolitiFact
claim: Claim that residential bills rose 267% misrepresents Bloomberg's wholesale-price data, though data centers are a real driver of higher costs in some areas.
method: Fact-check of Bloomberg data use.
notes: Read via search snippet only.

title: Complaint of the Maryland Office of People's Counsel against PJM's hybrid transmission cost allocation (with Nelson & Eiden affidavit)
author_org: Maryland Office of People's Counsel
claim: PJM's hybrid cost allocation spreads data-center-driven regional transmission (RTEP 2022 W3, 2024 W1, 2025 W1; >$22bn baseline) across the footprint, assigning Maryland customers costs unrelated to Maryland load growth.
method: Cost-allocation affidavit applying PJM's solution-based DFAX/hybrid method to approved RTEP projects.
region: PJM; Maryland (BGE, Pepco, Delmarva, Potomac Edison)
notes: Covered by Bloomberg (2026-05-07) as 'AI push to add $1.6 billion to Maryland power bills'. Transmission costs begin 2029, peak 2033.

title: PJM Board Annual Meeting: Maryland People's Counsel presentation on behalf of Consumer Advocates of PJM States (CAPS)
author_org: Maryland Office of People's Counsel / CAPS
claim: PJM wholesale costs are 55-70% of residential bills; PJM's 2026 forecast shows organic (non-data-center) load flat-to-negative for ten years, so data centers are the core cost driver and should be planned and charged separately.
method: Bill decomposition (BGE example) and PJM 2026 load forecast breakdown.

title: PJM Board to Decide on Higher Bills for 67 Million Americans Due to Data Centers
author_org: Natural Resources Defense Council (with Citizens Utility Board briefing)
claim: If data-center load keeps outrunning supply, PJM customers face about $163bn of capacity costs in 2028-2032 (through 2033) and recurring shortfalls; requiring data centers to bring their own capacity would cut costs by roughly $100bn.
method: Projection of PJM capacity prices/quantities under official large-load forecast (5-7 GW/yr) after the price cap expires.
notes: $163bn read on the NRDC release; the $27-30bn/yr, $70/month and $100bn figures come from CUB/E&E secondary summaries (UNVERIFIED).

title: Rapid Data Center Growth Risks Utility Bill & Emissions Increases in the Mid-Atlantic
author_org: Sierra Club
claim: Rapid data-center growth could raise average PJM residential bills about 10%, more in Virginia, and increase emissions.
method: Modeling based on PJM's 2022-era load forecast (per summary).
notes: Page redirected (HTTP 302) for scripts; figures from search snippet only. Sierra Club's 2027 legislative menu reports ~147 data-center guardrail bills in 34 states in 2026, ~25 passed (UNVERIFIED): https://www.sierraclub.org/sites/default/files/2026-08/2027-state-legislative-menu-for-data-center-guardrails.pdf

title: Retail rate trends in the US
author_org: Charles River Associates for Edison Electric Institute
claim: Data centers did not trigger retail rate increases, with one exception (PJM capacity prices, partly due to data centers); recent increases are concentrated in the Northeast (wholesale prices) and California (wildfires).
method: EIA state retail-rate trends, 5-year change to Oct 2025, timing comparison against data-center growth.
notes: Commissioned by the utility trade association.

title: America's Electric Companies Are Protecting Customers and Powering Innovation (statement on White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge expansion)
author_org: Edison Electric Institute
claim: Connecting data centers responsibly spreads costs over more customers; cites Georgia PSC approving ~ $50/yr lower rates and an Alliant Iowa five-year residential rate freeze tied to data-center growth.
method: Trade-association statement.
notes: Advocacy by utilities, which earn returns on new rate base built for data centers.

title: Have data centers raised your electric bill?
author_org: EPRI (Energy Systems and Climate Analysis)
claim: Causal evidence suggests data centers modestly lowered average US retail rates in 2015-2024 by spreading fixed costs over more demand.
method: Econometric (causal) analysis of 2015-2024 rates vs data-center load (per secondary summaries).
notes: URL returned 'page not found' to scripts; numbers from search snippets (incl. an LBNL literature review citing it). Backward-looking: does not cover the 2025+ PJM capacity shock.

title: The Effects of Load Growth on Electricity Prices in the United States: A Literature Review
author_org: Columbia University SIPA Center on Global Energy Policy (supported by Google.org)
claim: Residential prices rose more than twice inflation in 2025, breaking the 2019-2024 pattern; increases come from layered regional pressures (grid hardening, disasters, fuel, mandates) not demand alone; 'beneficiary-pays' tariffs are emerging to stop cost shifts.
method: Literature and data synthesis.
notes: Funded by Google.org (a data-center operator's philanthropy).

title: How the AI Data Center Boom Costs [Americans]: investigation of seven data-center operators
author_org: Offices of Sens. Warren, Van Hollen and Blumenthal
claim: Operators' 'fair share' pledges cover infrastructure built exclusively for their sites but not broader system upgrades; companies opposed 'but-for' cost allocation, seek NDAs and tax breaks, and play states against each other.
method: Congressional inquiry responses and staff interviews (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, CoreWeave, Digital Realty, Equinix).
notes: Partisan (Democratic senators') staff report; qualitative.

title: Working paper on county-level retail rates after data-center entry
author_org: Georgia Tech (working paper)
claim: Small average increase in retail electricity rates in a subset of US counties after initial data-center entry.
method: Event-study across counties (per E3 summary).
notes: Known only through E3's 2026 literature review; original paper not located.

title: State load growth vs retail rate changes
author_org: Bates White Economic Consulting
claim: States with the largest load increases (Texas, Virginia) had the smallest rate increases; California and New York had the largest increases with falling load.
method: State-level comparison (per E3 summary).
notes: Known only through E3's 2026 literature review.
